summary: How the gut tube is divided into foregut, midgut, and hindgut, how the midgut herniates and rotates, and how the liver, pancreas, and enteric nerves form. Exam questions link each step to the birth defect that results when it fails, and use the gut divisions to explain blood supply and referred pain.

notes.h: Three parts of the gut tube
points: Foregut: pharynx to the second part of the duodenum (at the major papilla), plus liver, gallbladder, and pancreas. Artery: celiac trunk.
Midgut: distal duodenum to the proximal two thirds of the transverse colon. Artery: superior mesenteric (SMA).
Hindgut: distal third of the transverse colon to the anal canal above the pectinate line. Artery: inferior mesenteric (IMA).
Visceral pain is dull and poorly localized and refers to the midline by gut division: foregut to the epigastrium, midgut to the umbilicus, hindgut to the suprapubic region.
Early appendicitis hurts at the umbilicus (midgut, T10) before it moves to the right lower quadrant once the parietal peritoneum is irritated.
notes.why: Each gut division is supplied by the unpaired aortic branch that grew with it, so the arterial boundaries match the embryologic ones at the major papilla and the distal transverse colon. Visceral afferents from each division travel with sympathetic fibers back to the spinal segments that supplied that part in the embryo, and the brain maps that input onto the matching midline dermatomes. Because the gut is a midline organ with bilateral innervation, the pain is dull, central, and poorly localized until inflammation reaches the somatically innervated parietal peritoneum, which is why appendicitis pain moves from the umbilicus to the right lower quadrant.

points: In week 6 the midgut loop grows faster than the abdomen and herniates into the umbilical cord (physiologic herniation).
The loop rotates 270 degrees counterclockwise (viewed from the front) around the axis of the SMA: 90 degrees while herniated, 180 degrees as it returns.
The loops return to the abdomen by about week 10, and the cecum descends to the right lower quadrant.
Malrotation leaves the cecum high and Ladd bands crossing the duodenum, and the narrow mesentery can twist (midgut volvulus) with bilious vomiting in a newborn.
Omphalocele: herniated loops fail to return, so viscera sit at the umbilicus in a sac of peritoneum and amnion.
notes.why: The midgut herniates because the fast-growing loop and the large fetal liver outgrow the abdominal cavity. Rotation uses the SMA as its axis, so normal rotation leaves the duodenojejunal flexure left of the SMA and the mesentery fixed on a long diagonal base. In malrotation the mesentery stays narrow and centered on the SMA, so the bowel can twist around it and cut off flow to the whole midgut, while Ladd bands can compress the duodenum. Omphalocele is failed return of the physiologic hernia, so the bowel stays inside a peritoneum and amnion sac.

points: In week 4 the respiratory diverticulum buds from the ventral foregut; the tracheoesophageal septum then separates trachea in front from esophagus behind.
A septum that deviates or fails gives esophageal atresia, tracheoesophageal fistula (TEF), or both.
Most common type: proximal esophageal atresia with a distal TEF, causing drooling, choking on first feeds, an NG tube that coils, and air in the stomach.
The hepatic diverticulum grows from the distal foregut into the septum transversum; endoderm forms hepatocytes and bile duct lining, and its caudal part forms the gallbladder and cystic duct.
Pancreas: dorsal bud forms most of the gland; ventral bud rotates behind the duodenum and forms the uncinate process and part of the head.
Annular pancreas: a bifid ventral bud wraps around the second part of the duodenum and can obstruct it.
Pancreas divisum: dorsal and ventral ducts fail to fuse, so most juice drains through the minor papilla.
notes.why: The tracheoesophageal septum splits one foregut tube into a ventral airway and a dorsal esophagus. When the septum deviates posteriorly, the esophagus ends blindly and its distal part stays joined to the trachea: saliva pools in the pouch, air reaches the stomach through the fistula, and the fetus cannot swallow amniotic fluid (polyhydramnios). The bile duct and ventral pancreatic duct bud from the same endoderm, so they end together at the major papilla. The dorsal duct drains at the minor papilla, so in pancreas divisum most juice must pass that small opening.

points: Neural crest cells migrate along the gut from cranial to caudal to form the myenteric and submucosal plexuses.
Hirschsprung disease: failed migration (often RET mutation) leaves a distal aganglionic segment that always includes the rectum and cannot relax.
Hirschsprung signs: no meconium in the first 48 hours, a dilated colon above the narrow segment, and an explosive stool after rectal exam; biopsy shows no ganglion cells.
The duodenal lumen is filled in by epithelial growth around weeks 5 to 6 and opens again (recanalizes) by the end of the embryonic period.
Failed recanalization gives duodenal atresia: bilious vomiting, a double bubble on X-ray, polyhydramnios, and a strong link to Down syndrome.
notes.why: Neural crest cells colonize the gut from cranial to caudal, so a migration failure always leaves the most distal bowel, including the rectum, without ganglia. RET encodes the receptor for glial cell line derived neurotrophic factor (GDNF), which keeps crest cells surviving and migrating. Without inhibitory neurons releasing nitric oxide and VIP, the segment stays contracted and the internal sphincter does not relax, so stool dilates the normal colon above. In duodenal atresia the epithelial plug never reopens, and because the block usually lies below the papilla, the vomitus contains bile.

tricks.label: 90 out, 180 back
tricks.text: The midgut turns 90 degrees counterclockwise while it is in the cord and 180 degrees more as it comes home, for 270 degrees in all around the SMA.

tricks.label: VACTERL
tricks.text: Vertebral defects, Anal atresia, Cardiac defects, TracheoEsophageal fistula, Renal anomalies, Limb anomalies. A baby with a TEF gets checked for the rest.

tricks.label: Follow the artery to the pain
tricks.text: Name the artery that feeds the organ and you know where its pain refers: celiac to the epigastrium, SMA to the umbilicus, IMA to the suprapubic area.

highYield: Duodenal atresia with a double bubble points to Down syndrome; jejunal and ileal atresia come from a vascular accident instead.
Hirschsprung disease is also more common in Down syndrome, and the rectum is always involved.
Omphalocele is linked to trisomies 13 and 18 and Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome; gastroschisis has no covering sac.
The H-type TEF (no atresia) shows up later as recurrent aspiration pneumonia.
An annular pancreas and duodenal atresia both obstruct the second part of the duodenum; the vomiting is bilious when the block lies below the major papilla, as it usually does.
The spleen comes from mesoderm in the dorsal mesogastrium yet is supplied by the celiac trunk (splenic artery).
pitfalls: Omphalocele is midline and covered by a sac; gastroschisis is usually right of the umbilicus with bare bowel and no sac.
Malrotation is a rotation problem; omphalocele is a return problem. Both involve the midgut.
The foregut ends at the major duodenal papilla, so the duodenum above the papilla hurts like the stomach and the duodenum below it like the small bowel.
The ventral pancreatic bud forms the uncinate process; the dorsal bud forms the body and tail.

flows.title: Midgut herniation and rotation
steps: Week 6: the fast-growing midgut loop herniates into the umbilical cord.
The loop rotates 90 degrees counterclockwise around the superior mesenteric artery.
By about week 10 the loops return, rotating another 180 degrees.
The total 270 degrees leaves the duodenojejunal flexure left of the SMA.
The cecum descends to the right lower quadrant and the mesentery fixes broadly.

flows.title: Hirschsprung disease
steps: Loss of RET signaling (often a RET mutation) impairs neural crest migration.
Crest cells fail to reach the distal bowel, always including the rectum.
The aganglionic segment lacks inhibitory neurons that release nitric oxide and VIP.
The segment stays contracted and the internal sphincter cannot relax.
Stool backs up, dilating normal colon above; meconium is delayed past 48 hours.

flows.title: Duodenal atresia
steps: Weeks 5 to 6: epithelial growth temporarily plugs the duodenal lumen.
The plug fails to vacuolize and recanalize, leaving a complete obstruction.
The fetus cannot pass swallowed amniotic fluid, causing polyhydramnios.
After birth, a block usually below the papilla causes bilious vomiting.
Air in the stomach and proximal duodenum gives the double bubble sign.

summary: The microscopic structure of the gut wall, stomach glands, small and large intestine, liver, pancreas, and salivary glands. Exam questions show a cell or a section and ask what it secretes, where it is, and what happens when it is damaged.

notes.h: Four layers of the gut wall
points: Mucosa: epithelium, lamina propria, and a thin muscularis mucosae.
Submucosa: dense connective tissue with vessels and the submucosal (Meissner) plexus, which controls secretion and local blood flow.
Muscularis externa: inner circular and outer longitudinal smooth muscle, with the myenteric (Auerbach) plexus between them controlling motility.
Outer layer: serosa (mesothelium) over intraperitoneal parts; adventitia over the thoracic esophagus and retroperitoneal parts.
notes.why: Each plexus sits next to what it controls: the submucosal plexus beside the mucosal glands and vessels, and the myenteric plexus between the two muscle coats it coordinates. The inner circular layer narrows the lumen and the outer longitudinal layer shortens the segment, and the myenteric plexus sequences the two to produce peristalsis. The outer layer depends on the peritoneum: organs suspended in the peritoneal cavity are covered by mesothelium (serosa), while fixed structures are anchored by loose connective tissue (adventitia), which is one reason esophageal cancer spreads easily into the mediastinum.

points: Esophagus: nonkeratinized stratified squamous to resist abrasion.
Stomach through colon: simple columnar for secretion and absorption.
Anal canal: columnar above the pectinate line and stratified squamous below it.
Barrett esophagus: chronic acid reflux turns distal esophageal squamous epithelium into intestinal-type columnar epithelium with goblet cells, which raises adenocarcinoma risk.
notes.why: Each epithelium matches its local stress: stratified squamous cells resist friction from food in the esophagus and stool in the lower anal canal, while single columnar cells elsewhere secrete and absorb. The pectinate line marks where hindgut endoderm meets the ectoderm of the proctodeum, so the change in epithelium there comes with changes in blood supply, lymph drainage, and nerves. In Barrett esophagus, repeated acid and bile injury drives metaplasia, a switch to a cell type that resists acid better, and goblet cells confirm intestinal metaplasia on biopsy. The metaplastic epithelium can progress through dysplasia to adenocarcinoma.

points: Parietal cells (body and fundus): pink, fried-egg look; secrete HCl and intrinsic factor.
Chief cells (base of body and fundus glands): basophilic; secrete pepsinogen.
Mucous neck cells: mucus; surface mucous cells also add bicarbonate.
G cells (antrum): gastrin. D cells: somatostatin. ECL cells: histamine.
Autoimmune gastritis destroys body and fundus mucosa, so acid, intrinsic factor, and pepsinogen all fall while the antrum is spared.
Without acid feedback, antral G cells keep releasing gastrin (hypergastrinemia), and lost intrinsic factor leads to vitamin B12 deficiency (pernicious anemia).
notes.why: Parietal cells stain pink from the mitochondria that power the H+/K+ ATPase, and chief cells are basophilic from the rough endoplasmic reticulum that makes pepsinogen. In autoimmune gastritis, T cells and autoantibodies target the H+/K+ ATPase and intrinsic factor, so body and fundus glands are lost and achlorhydria follows. Low antral pH normally releases somatostatin to restrain G cells; without acid, gastrin rises and drives ECL cell hyperplasia, which can progress to carcinoid tumors. Lost intrinsic factor blocks B12 uptake in the terminal ileum, causing megaloblastic anemia and spinal cord degeneration.

points: Duodenum: Brunner glands in the submucosa secrete alkaline mucus to neutralize acid.
Jejunum: tall, closely spaced plicae circulares and long villi; the main absorptive segment.
Ileum: Peyer patches (lymphoid follicles with overlying M cells) in the lamina propria and submucosa.
Small intestine crypts hold stem cells and Paneth cells (lysozyme and defensins).
Colon: no villi, straight crypts packed with goblet cells, and outer longitudinal muscle gathered into taeniae coli.
notes.why: Each segment's structure matches its job. Brunner glands lie where acidic chyme first arrives, and their alkaline mucus protects the duodenal mucosa until pancreatic bicarbonate neutralizes the acid. The jejunum has the most surface area from tall folds and long villi, so most nutrient absorption happens there, while the ileum faces more bacteria and carries Peyer patches, where M cells sample antigens and start mucosal IgA responses. The colon mainly absorbs water and salt and lubricates drying stool, which explains why it has no villi and so many goblet cells.

points: Classic lobule: a hexagon with a central vein in the middle and portal triads (portal vein branch, hepatic artery branch, bile duct) at the corners.
Blood runs from the triads through fenestrated sinusoids to the central vein; bile runs the other way in canaliculi toward the triad.
Space of Disse: the gap between hepatocytes and sinusoid lining, where plasma meets hepatocyte microvilli.
Kupffer cells are sinusoid macrophages; stellate (Ito) cells in the space of Disse store vitamin A and make collagen in fibrosis.
Acinus zones: zone 1 near the triad gets the most oxygen; zone 3 near the central vein gets the least and has the most cytochrome P450.
Zone 3 dies first in shock or heart failure and in acetaminophen overdose (toxic metabolite NAPQI made by P450).
notes.why: Blood enters the acinus at the portal triad and flows toward the central vein, so zone 1 hepatocytes get blood rich in oxygen and nutrients first and zone 3 gets what is left. Zone 3 therefore has the lowest oxygen tension and dies first when perfusion falls. Zone 3 cells also have the most CYP2E1, so they make the most NAPQI from acetaminophen, and once glutathione is used up NAPQI binds cell proteins and causes centrilobular necrosis. In chronic injury, signals such as TGF-beta from Kupffer cells and damaged hepatocytes activate stellate cells into myofibroblasts, which lay collagen in the space of Disse and block exchange between sinusoid and hepatocyte.

points: Pancreatic acini: basophilic base and apical eosinophilic zymogen granules; centroacinar cells start the ducts.
Islets of Langerhans: pale clusters of endocrine cells scattered among the acini.
Serous acini stain dark and make watery protein-rich (amylase) secretion; mucous acini look pale and foamy.
Parotid is mainly serous, submandibular is mixed (mostly serous), and sublingual is mostly mucous.
notes.why: Acinar cells are built for protein export: rough endoplasmic reticulum at the base makes enzymes, and zymogen granules store them at the apex until secretion. Centroacinar and duct cells add bicarbonate-rich fluid through CFTR and chloride-bicarbonate exchange, which flushes the enzymes into the duodenum. Serous cells stain dark because they are full of protein-making machinery and granules, while mucous cells look pale because the mucin they store washes out during routine tissue processing. Islets look pale against the acini because their endocrine cells lack the dense rough endoplasmic reticulum of acinar cells, and they release hormones into capillaries with no duct.

tricks.label: Brunner in the bulb
tricks.text: Brunner glands mean duodenum. Think B for bicarbonate-rich mucus that buffers acid as it leaves the stomach.

tricks.label: Zone 3 is last in line
tricks.text: Blood reaches zone 3 last, after the oxygen is used up, and zone 3 holds the most P450. Low oxygen and toxic drug metabolites both hit it first.

tricks.label: Parotid is pure
tricks.text: The parotid is almost entirely serous, so its acini all stain dark. Pale foamy mucous acini mean submandibular or sublingual.

highYield: Autoimmune gastritis: anti-parietal cell and anti-intrinsic factor antibodies, achlorhydria, high gastrin, and B12 deficiency.
Barrett esophagus is intestinal metaplasia with goblet cells and is the precursor of esophageal adenocarcinoma.
Stellate (Ito) cells drive liver fibrosis and cirrhosis by laying down collagen in the space of Disse.
Acetaminophen overdose causes centrilobular (zone 3) necrosis.
Peyer patches in the ileum are the entry point for some invasive bacteria (for example Salmonella Typhi) through M cells.
Paneth cells at crypt bases release defensins and lysozyme.
pitfalls: Meissner (submucosal) plexus controls secretion; Auerbach (myenteric) plexus controls motility.
Zone 1 is near the portal triad, and zone 3 is near the central vein; the lobule is drawn around the central vein while the acinus is drawn around the triad.
Autoimmune gastritis spares the antrum, so gastrin rises; H. pylori gastritis usually starts in the antrum.
Brunner glands sit in the submucosa; crypts of Lieberkuhn sit in the mucosa.

steps: Autoimmunity targets the parietal cell H+/K+ ATPase and intrinsic factor.
Body and fundus glands atrophy while the antrum is spared.

flows.title: Acetaminophen injury in zone 3
steps: Overdose saturates the glucuronidation and sulfation pathways.
More drug is oxidized by CYP2E1, most abundant in zone 3 hepatocytes.
CYP2E1 converts acetaminophen to the reactive metabolite NAPQI.
Glutathione is used up, so NAPQI binds hepatocyte proteins.

summary: The gross anatomy of the stomach, duodenum, liver, biliary tree, colon, and salivary glands, and which organs lie behind the peritoneum. Exam questions use location to explain where a stone blocks, where an injury bleeds, and which nerve is at risk.

points: Stomach parts: cardia, fundus, body, antrum, and pylorus, with a lesser and a greater curvature.
Duodenum is about 25 cm long and wraps in a C around the head of the pancreas.
First (superior) part: the duodenal bulb, the most common site of duodenal ulcers.
Second (descending) part: the major duodenal papilla, where bile and pancreatic juice enter.
Third (horizontal) part: crossed in front by the superior mesenteric vessels, with the aorta behind.
Fourth (ascending) part: ends at the duodenojejunal flexure, held by the suspensory ligament (of Treitz).
notes.why: The duodenal bulb receives acidic chyme straight from the pylorus before pancreatic bicarbonate enters at the papilla, which is why most duodenal ulcers form in the first part. The second part sits where foregut meets midgut, so the bile duct, pancreatic ducts, and the papilla cluster there. The third part runs in the angle between the aorta and the SMA, so if that angle narrows (for example after rapid weight loss shrinks the fat pad), the duodenum can be compressed in superior mesenteric artery syndrome. The suspensory ligament at the duodenojejunal flexure is the landmark that divides upper from lower GI bleeding.

points: Intraperitoneal organs hang on a mesentery and are wrapped in visceral peritoneum: stomach, jejunum, ileum, transverse and sigmoid colon, liver, spleen.
Retroperitoneal gut structures: duodenum parts 2 to 4, pancreas except the tail, ascending and descending colon, and part of the rectum.
Retroperitoneal organs are fixed to the back wall, so bleeding from them can collect without peritoneal signs.
The first part of the duodenum is mostly intraperitoneal; the pancreatic tail runs in the splenorenal ligament.
notes.why: Organs are classified by how they relate to the peritoneum during development. Organs that kept a mesentery stay intraperitoneal and mobile, while the duodenum, ascending colon, and descending colon were pressed against the posterior wall and their mesenteries fused with the parietal peritoneum, making them secondarily retroperitoneal. Because retroperitoneal organs lie outside the peritoneal cavity, injury or bleeding there (for example duodenal rupture or hemorrhagic pancreatitis) may show as back or flank pain and flank bruising with few signs of peritonitis.

points: Anatomic lobes: right and left (split by the falciform ligament), plus the caudate and quadrate lobes on the underside.
Bare area: the posterior surface touching the diaphragm, with no peritoneal cover.
Porta hepatis: the hilum where the portal vein and hepatic artery enter and the hepatic ducts leave.
Bile path: right and left hepatic ducts, common hepatic duct, joined by the cystic duct to form the common bile duct.
The common bile duct runs behind the first part of the duodenum and through the pancreatic head, then joins the main pancreatic duct at the ampulla of Vater.
The sphincter of Oddi controls flow from the ampulla into the second part of the duodenum.
notes.why: The liver grows into the ventral mesentery, so its peritoneal folds (falciform, coronary, and triangular ligaments and the lesser omentum) are remnants of that mesentery, and the bare area lies between the separated layers of the coronary ligament directly on the diaphragm. The bile duct and pancreatic duct share a final channel at the ampulla, so a gallstone impacted there can block both and cause obstructive jaundice with gallstone pancreatitis. Cholecystokinin contracts the gallbladder and relaxes the sphincter of Oddi at the same time, so bile reaches the duodenum when fat arrives.

points: Colon has three taeniae coli (bands of longitudinal muscle), haustra (sacculations), and omental appendices (fat tags); small intestine has none of these.
The taeniae converge at the base of the appendix, which surgeons follow to find it.
McBurney point: one third of the way from the right anterior superior iliac spine to the umbilicus, the surface mark for the appendix base.
notes.why: In the colon the outer longitudinal muscle is gathered into three bands that are shorter than the bowel wall, so the wall puckers into haustra. The three taeniae run along the colon and converge on the cecum at the root of the appendix, which makes them a reliable guide to the base even though the tip varies in position (often retrocecal). McBurney point marks this base on the skin, and tenderness appears there once inflammation reaches the overlying parietal peritoneum.

points: Parotid: largest, in front of the ear over the masseter; its duct crosses the masseter, pierces the buccinator, and opens opposite the upper second molar.
Submandibular: under the mandible; its duct opens beside the lingual frenulum. Most salivary stones form here.
Sublingual: in the floor of the mouth, with many small ducts.
The facial nerve (CN VII) runs through the parotid and splits into its five branches there, so a parotid tumor or surgery can cause facial weakness.
notes.why: The facial nerve leaves the stylomastoid foramen, enters the parotid, and divides into its terminal branches inside the gland, so a parotid tumor or parotid surgery can paralyze the muscles of facial expression on that side. Facial weakness with a parotid mass is a warning sign of malignancy, because benign tumors such as pleomorphic adenoma usually push the nerve aside without invading it. Stones form most often in the submandibular gland because its saliva is more alkaline and richer in mucin, and its long duct runs upward against gravity to the floor of the mouth.

tricks.label: SAD PUCKER
tricks.text: Retroperitoneal structures: Suprarenal glands, Aorta and IVC, Duodenum (parts 2 to 4), Pancreas (except tail), Ureters, Colon (ascending and descending), Kidneys, Esophagus (lower part), Rectum (partly).

tricks.label: Follow the bands
tricks.text: Taeniae coli mean colon. Trace them down the cecum and they meet at the base of the appendix, wherever its tip has wandered.

tricks.label: One stone, two blocks
tricks.text: A stone stuck at the ampulla blocks the common bile duct and the pancreatic duct at once, so jaundice and pancreatitis can arrive together.

highYield: A stone in the common bile duct gives obstructive jaundice; a stone at the ampulla can also cause gallstone pancreatitis.
Pancreatic head cancer compresses the common bile duct and causes painless jaundice with a palpable gallbladder (Courvoisier sign).
Compression of the third part of the duodenum between the SMA and aorta (SMA syndrome) can follow rapid weight loss.
Facial nerve weakness with a parotid mass suggests a malignant tumor; the common pleomorphic adenoma rarely affects the nerve.
Blunt trauma can crush the retroperitoneal duodenum or pancreas against the spine.
The appendix base is constant at the taeniae meeting point; the tip is often retrocecal.
pitfalls: The major papilla (bile and main pancreatic duct) is in the second part of the duodenum; the minor papilla, slightly higher, drains the accessory duct.
Ascending and descending colon are retroperitoneal; transverse and sigmoid colon have mesenteries and are intraperitoneal.
The bare area of the liver touches the diaphragm directly, with no peritoneum between them.
The facial nerve passes through the parotid without supplying it; the parotid gets secretomotor fibers from CN IX.

flows.title: Path of bile from liver to duodenum
steps: Hepatocytes secrete bile into canaliculi that drain to ducts in the portal triads.
Right and left hepatic ducts join to form the common hepatic duct.
The cystic duct joins it to form the common bile duct.
The common bile duct passes behind the duodenal bulb and through the pancreatic head.
It joins the main pancreatic duct at the ampulla of Vater.
Bile enters the second part of the duodenum through the sphincter of Oddi.

flows.title: Path of the parotid duct
steps: Saliva leaves the parotid gland, which lies in front of the ear.
The duct runs forward across the surface of the masseter.
At the front edge of the masseter it pierces the buccinator.
It opens into the mouth opposite the upper second molar.

summary: Where the gut sits in the mouth, mediastinum, and abdominopelvic cavity: the path and narrowings of the esophagus, nerve supply of the tongue, peritoneal sacs and ligaments, the inguinal region, and the low spaces where fluid pools. Exam questions give a lesion or a collection and ask which structure or space is involved.

points: Starts at the cricoid cartilage (C6) as a continuation of the pharynx.
Runs through the superior and then posterior mediastinum, behind the trachea and the left atrium.
Passes through the esophageal hiatus of the diaphragm at T10 with the vagal trunks.
Three narrowings: the cricopharyngeus (upper esophageal sphincter), the crossing of the aortic arch and left main bronchus, and the diaphragmatic hiatus.
Swallowed objects and pills tend to lodge at these narrowings, and an enlarged left atrium can press on the esophagus.
notes.why: The esophagus starts at the cricopharyngeus at C6 and descends against the aortic arch, the left main bronchus, and the left atrium. At each narrowing a muscle ring or an outside structure limits stretch, so a bolus or pill that stays in contact can lodge and cause impaction or pill esophagitis. Because the left atrium lies directly in front, left atrial enlargement (for example in mitral stenosis) can indent the esophagus and cause dysphagia. Since the stomach rotated in development, the left vagus forms the anterior trunk and the right vagus the posterior trunk at the hiatus.

points: Anterior two thirds: touch by CN V3 (lingual nerve); taste by CN VII (chorda tympani riding with the lingual nerve).
Posterior third: touch and taste by CN IX.
Motor: CN XII to all tongue muscles except palatoglossus, which is CN X.
A lower motor neuron CN XII lesion makes the protruded tongue deviate toward the injured side, with atrophy and fasciculations on that side.
Lingual nerve injury above where the chorda tympani joins it removes touch only; injury below the junction removes both touch and taste from the anterior two thirds.
notes.why: Tongue innervation follows its development: the anterior two thirds come from the first pharyngeal arch (V3) and the posterior third from the third arch (CN IX), while the muscles come from occipital somites that bring CN XII. Chorda tympani taste fibers join the lingual nerve in the infratemporal fossa, so the level of a lingual nerve injury decides whether taste is lost. Palatoglossus develops with the palatal muscles, which the vagus supplies. In a lower motor neuron CN XII lesion, the healthy genioglossus pushes unopposed, so the tongue deviates toward the weak side.

points: Greater sac: most of the peritoneal cavity. Lesser sac (omental bursa): behind the stomach and lesser omentum.
The two sacs connect through the omental (epiploic) foramen, whose front edge is the hepatoduodenal ligament.
Lesser omentum: hepatogastric (gastrohepatic) plus hepatoduodenal ligaments. Greater omentum hangs from the greater curvature.
Hepatoduodenal ligament carries the portal triad: portal vein behind, proper hepatic artery in front on the left, common bile duct in front on the right.
Squeezing this ligament (Pringle maneuver) controls bleeding from the liver.
notes.why: The lesser sac forms when the stomach rotates and its dorsal mesentery bulges to the left, trapping a space behind the stomach that opens to the greater sac only through the omental foramen. The free edge of the lesser omentum forms the front wall of that foramen and carries the portal triad, because the liver grew into the ventral mesentery and its vessels and duct reach it through that edge. Squeezing this edge (Pringle maneuver) stops inflow from both the hepatic artery and the portal vein, so bleeding that continues points to the hepatic veins or the IVC, which lie outside the clamp.

points: The inguinal canal runs from the deep ring (in transversalis fascia, lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels) to the superficial ring (in external oblique aponeurosis).
Hesselbach triangle: inferior epigastric vessels laterally, rectus abdominis medially, inguinal ligament below.
Indirect hernia: enters the deep ring lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels through a patent processus vaginalis and can reach the scrotum; most common type, often in young males.
Direct hernia: pushes through a weak Hesselbach triangle medial to the vessels; usually older men.
Femoral hernia: below the inguinal ligament through the femoral canal; more common in women and most likely to strangulate.
notes.why: The deep ring is the opening in the transversalis fascia where the processus vaginalis led the testis (or the round ligament) into the canal, so an indirect hernia follows a congenital path along the spermatic cord, starting lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels. A direct hernia is acquired: with age the transversalis fascia in the Hesselbach triangle weakens, and abdominal pressure pushes viscera straight through medial to the vessels. The femoral ring is narrow and rigid, bounded by the inguinal, lacunar, and pectineal ligaments, so a femoral hernia is the type most likely to become incarcerated and strangulate.

points: Supine: the hepatorenal recess (Morison pouch) is the lowest part of the upper abdomen, so blood and pus pool there.
Upright: the rectouterine pouch (Douglas) in women or the rectovesical pouch in men is the lowest point of the peritoneal cavity.
Subphrenic spaces under the diaphragm collect abscesses after perforation or surgery, sometimes with shoulder-tip pain from phrenic nerve irritation.
The paracolic gutters let fluid travel between the pelvis and the upper abdomen.
notes.why: Peritoneal fluid moves with gravity along the paths set by peritoneal attachments, so it gathers in the lowest recess for the patient's position. Supine, the hepatorenal recess is the most dependent upper abdominal space, which is why a FAST ultrasound examines Morison pouch for blood after trauma. Upright, fluid runs down the paracolic gutters to the pelvis, so pelvic abscesses from appendicitis or salpingitis form in the rectouterine or rectovesical pouch, where a rectal or vaginal exam can reach them. A subphrenic abscess irritates diaphragmatic peritoneum supplied by the phrenic nerve (C3 to C5), so pain is referred to the shoulder tip, which shares those cord segments.

tricks.label: MDs don't LIe
tricks.text: Medial to the inferior epigastric vessels is a Direct hernia; Lateral is Indirect.

tricks.label: Lick your wounds
tricks.text: A hypoglossal lesion pushes the tongue toward the hurt side, because the healthy genioglossus pushes forward alone.

highYield: Gag reflex: afferent CN IX, efferent CN X.
An indirect inguinal hernia follows the path of testicular descent and is covered by all three layers of spermatic fascia.
In a supine trauma patient, free fluid on a FAST exam most often shows up first in the hepatorenal recess.
A ruptured appendix can track pus up the right paracolic gutter to the right subphrenic space.
The omental foramen lies behind the hepatoduodenal ligament and in front of the IVC.
Third molar extraction can injure the lingual nerve and cause loss of touch and taste on the front of the tongue.
pitfalls: Palatoglossus is the one tongue muscle supplied by CN X; every other tongue muscle is CN XII.
Taste and touch on the anterior two thirds travel in different nerves (VII and V3), while the posterior third uses CN IX for both.
Femoral hernias are more common in women than in men, yet indirect inguinal hernia is still the most common hernia in women.
The hepatorenal recess is lowest when lying flat; the rectouterine or rectovesical pouch is lowest when upright.

flows.title: Course of the esophagus
steps: Begins at the cricopharyngeus (upper sphincter) at C6, the first narrowing.
Descends through the superior mediastinum behind the trachea.
Crossed by the aortic arch and left main bronchus, the second narrowing.
Runs through the posterior mediastinum behind the left atrium.
Passes the diaphragmatic hiatus at T10 with the vagal trunks, the third narrowing.
Joins the cardia of the stomach.

flows.title: Path of an indirect inguinal hernia
steps: The processus vaginalis stays open after the testis descends.
Viscera enter the deep ring, lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels.
The sac travels through the inguinal canal inside the spermatic cord coverings.
It leaves through the superficial ring in the external oblique aponeurosis.
It can descend into the scrotum.

summary: The arteries that feed the gut, the portal vein that drains it, the shortcuts portal blood takes when the liver is blocked, and the two blood supplies of the anal canal and liver. Exam questions ask which vessel bleeds, which segment of colon dies in shock, and where varices form.

points: Leaves the aorta at about T12 and splits into the left gastric, splenic, and common hepatic arteries.
Left gastric supplies the lesser curvature and lower esophagus.
Splenic runs along the top of the pancreas and gives short gastric, left gastroepiploic, and pancreatic branches.
Common hepatic gives the proper hepatic artery (to the liver and, through the cystic artery, the gallbladder) and the gastroduodenal artery.
The gastroduodenal artery runs behind the first part of the duodenum, so a posterior duodenal ulcer can erode it and cause major bleeding.
notes.why: The celiac trunk supplies every foregut derivative, and the stomach gets paired arteries along each curvature that anastomose (left and right gastric on the lesser curvature, left and right gastroepiploic on the greater), so the stomach rarely infarcts. The location of an ulcer predicts which vessel bleeds: a posterior duodenal bulb ulcer erodes the gastroduodenal artery behind it, while a lesser curvature gastric ulcer erodes the left gastric artery. Anterior duodenal ulcers have no large artery behind them and are more likely to perforate, causing free air under the diaphragm.

points: SMA (about L1) supplies the distal duodenum to the proximal two thirds of the transverse colon through jejunal, ileal, ileocolic, right colic, and middle colic branches.
IMA (about L3) supplies the distal transverse colon to the upper rectum through left colic, sigmoid, and superior rectal branches.
The marginal artery runs along the colon and links SMA and IMA branches.
Watershed zones sit where two territories meet: the splenic flexure (SMA and IMA) and the rectosigmoid junction (sigmoid and superior rectal arteries).
Hypotension starves these watershed zones first and causes ischemic colitis: cramping pain followed by bloody diarrhea.
notes.why: Arterial territories follow the embryonic gut divisions, and the marginal artery and other collaterals link them, so a slowly narrowing artery can be bypassed. Watershed zones lie at the far ends of two territories where the collateral link is thin (Griffiths point at the splenic flexure, Sudeck point at the rectosigmoid), so perfusion pressure there is lowest and a global fall in flow starves them first. The mucosa is injured before the deeper layers because it has the highest metabolic demand and sits at the end of the arterial supply, so ischemic mucosa sloughs and bleeds, causing pain followed by bloody diarrhea.

points: The superior mesenteric vein and splenic vein join behind the neck of the pancreas to form the portal vein; the inferior mesenteric vein usually drains into the splenic vein.
The portal vein rises in the hepatoduodenal ligament to the porta hepatis.
Portal blood mixes with hepatic arterial blood in the sinusoids, drains to central veins, then hepatic veins, then the IVC.
Portal hypertension (often from cirrhosis) forces blood through portosystemic anastomoses back to the systemic veins.
notes.why: The portal vein collects blood from the capillary beds of the gut, spleen, and pancreas, so absorbed nutrients, drugs, and bacterial products pass through the liver before reaching the systemic circulation (first-pass metabolism). The portal system has no valves and lies between two capillary beds, so a rise in resistance in or beyond the liver raises pressure throughout it. Cirrhosis raises intrahepatic resistance through fibrosis and sinusoidal narrowing, so the spleen congests and blood is diverted through low-resistance portosystemic channels. Shunted blood bypasses hepatic clearance, which is why ammonia and other gut-derived toxins reach the brain in hepatic encephalopathy.

points: Esophagus: left gastric vein to esophageal veins draining to the azygos system. Result: esophageal varices that can bleed massively.
Umbilicus: paraumbilical veins to superficial veins of the abdominal wall. Result: caput medusae.
Rectum: superior rectal vein (portal) to middle and inferior rectal veins (systemic). Result: anorectal varices.
notes.why: Each anastomosis is a place where a portal tributary meets a systemic vein, and in health these channels carry little flow. When portal pressure rises (a hepatic venous pressure gradient above about 10 mmHg is clinically significant portal hypertension), blood reverses through them toward the lower-pressure systemic veins, and thin-walled submucosal veins dilate into varices. Esophageal varices are the most dangerous because they lie in the submucosa with little surrounding support, so they can rupture and bleed massively. At the umbilicus, paraumbilical veins in the falciform ligament carry portal blood to abdominal wall veins, so flow radiates away from the navel as caput medusae.

notes.h: Anal canal above and below the pectinate line
points: Above: columnar epithelium, superior rectal artery, portal drainage, internal iliac nodes, visceral (painless) nerves.
Below: stratified squamous epithelium, inferior rectal artery, systemic drainage, superficial inguinal nodes, somatic pudendal nerve (painful).
Internal hemorrhoids arise above the line and bleed without pain; external hemorrhoids arise below and hurt.
notes.why: The pectinate line marks where hindgut endoderm meets proctodeal ectoderm, so tissue above it is supplied like gut and tissue below it like skin. Above the line, visceral afferents respond to stretch and not to cutting, so internal hemorrhoids and tumors there are painless, while somatic inferior rectal nerves (pudendal branches) below the line make fissures and thrombosed external hemorrhoids very painful. The same boundary predicts spread: adenocarcinoma above the line drains to internal iliac nodes, while squamous cell carcinoma below it drains to superficial inguinal nodes, which can be felt in the groin.

notes.h: Two blood supplies to the liver
points: About 75% of liver blood flow comes from the portal vein and about 25% from the hepatic artery; each supplies roughly half of the oxygen.
Because two sources feed the liver, a block in one rarely causes hepatic infarction.
Bile ducts depend on the hepatic artery alone, so hepatic artery thrombosis (for example after liver transplant) causes bile duct ischemia and strictures.
notes.why: The liver receives about a quarter of cardiac output, and its two inflows reach the same sinusoids, so if one source fails the other can still perfuse and oxygenate hepatocytes. The hepatic arterial buffer response adds protection: when portal flow falls, adenosine that is normally washed away builds up around hepatic arterioles and dilates them, raising arterial inflow. The bile ducts lack this backup because their peribiliary capillary plexus is fed only by hepatic artery branches, so arterial occlusion causes ischemic biliary strictures even when hepatocytes survive.

tricks.label: Three exits for trapped portal blood
tricks.text: Portal blood escapes at the top (esophagus), the middle (umbilicus), and the bottom (rectum) of the gut. Varices, caput medusae, and anorectal varices are the same problem at three sites.

tricks.label: Watershed = border towns
tricks.text: Ischemia hits where two arterial territories meet and neither supplies much: splenic flexure and rectosigmoid junction.

tricks.label: Posterior bleeds, anterior perforates
tricks.text: A posterior duodenal ulcer erodes the gastroduodenal artery and bleeds; an anterior ulcer perforates into the peritoneal cavity and gives free air.

highYield: Massive upper GI bleeding from a posterior duodenal ulcer comes from the gastroduodenal artery.
A gastric ulcer on the lesser curvature can erode the left gastric artery.
Ischemic colitis after hypotension favors the splenic flexure; the rectum is spared by its dual supply.
Acute mesenteric ischemia (often an embolus to the SMA in atrial fibrillation) causes pain out of proportion to the exam.
Bleeding esophageal varices are a leading cause of death in cirrhosis.
Anal cancer below the pectinate line spreads to superficial inguinal nodes.
pitfalls: Anorectal varices come from portal hypertension; internal hemorrhoids are enlarged anal vascular cushions with other causes such as straining.
The inferior mesenteric vein drains into the splenic vein, while the SMV and splenic vein form the portal vein.
The portal vein brings most of the liver's blood flow, yet the hepatic artery is the only supply to the bile ducts.
The superior rectal artery comes from the IMA; the middle and inferior rectal arteries come from the internal iliac system.

summary: How food is chewed, swallowed, moved, broken down, and absorbed, how acid and gut hormones are controlled, and how defecation and vomiting work. Exam questions give a meal, a drug, or a lesion and ask you to predict the hormone, secretion, or acid-base change that follows.

points: Masseter, temporalis, medial and lateral pterygoids chew; all are supplied by CN V3.
Oral phase is voluntary: the tongue pushes the bolus into the pharynx.

Pharyngeal and esophageal phases are reflexes run by the swallowing center in the medulla: the soft palate seals the nose, the larynx rises, breathing pauses, and the upper esophageal sphincter opens.
Vagal inhibitory neurons release nitric oxide and VIP to relax the lower esophageal sphincter and the proximal stomach (receptive relaxation).
notes.why: Swallowing becomes a reflex once the bolus touches pharyngeal receptors, whose afferents (mainly CN IX and X) reach the swallowing center in the medulla and lower pons, which then runs a fixed motor sequence through CN V, IX, X, and XII. The sequence protects the airway: the soft palate closes the nasopharynx, the larynx rises under the epiglottis, the vocal folds close, and breathing stops briefly while the upper sphincter opens. The lower esophageal sphincter relaxes ahead of the peristaltic wave because vagal inhibitory neurons release nitric oxide and VIP. In achalasia these inhibitory neurons are lost, so the sphincter cannot relax and the esophageal body loses peristalsis.

notes.h: Slow waves, peristalsis, and the MMC
points: Interstitial cells of Cajal make slow waves that set the maximum contraction rate (about 3 per minute in the stomach, about 12 per minute in the duodenum).
Contraction happens only when spike potentials fire on top of a slow wave; ACh and stretch make this more likely.
Peristalsis needs the myenteric plexus: contraction above the bolus (ACh, substance P) and relaxation below it (VIP, nitric oxide).
Between meals, motilin from M cells drives the migrating motor complex about every 90 minutes to sweep the stomach and small bowel clean; eating stops it.
notes.why: Interstitial cells of Cajal make slow waves that spread to smooth muscle through gap junctions, but contraction needs spike potentials, which fire only when a slow wave crest passes threshold and let calcium enter. Nerves and hormones therefore set contraction strength, while slow wave frequency sets the maximum rate. Peristalsis is a local myenteric reflex (the law of the gut), so it still works after vagotomy but fails where ganglia are missing. The MMC sweeps debris and bacteria out between meals, so when it fails (diabetic neuropathy, scleroderma), small intestinal bacterial overgrowth can follow.

points: Parietal cell stimulators: ACh (M3), gastrin (CCK-B), and histamine (H2); each makes the others stronger.
Gastrin also acts by making ECL cells release histamine.
Final step: the H+/K+ ATPase pumps H+ into the lumen in exchange for K+.
Somatostatin from D cells, released when antral pH falls, inhibits G cells and parietal cells.
Cephalic phase (about 30%): sight, smell, and chewing drive the vagus, which releases ACh and GRP (gastrin releasing peptide).
Gastric phase (about 60%): stretch and peptides in the stomach release gastrin.
Intestinal phase (about 10%): protein in the duodenum releases a little gastrin, but acid and fat in the duodenum mainly inhibit acid through secretin, GIP, and nerve reflexes.
notes.why: Histamine acts on the parietal cell through H2 receptors and cAMP, while acetylcholine and gastrin act through M3 and CCK-B receptors and calcium, so together they produce more acid than the sum of each (potentiation). This is why an H2 blocker also blunts the response to ACh and gastrin, while a proton pump inhibitor blocks the shared final step. Each phase is named for where the signal starts: the head, the stomach, or the duodenum, where acid and fat mainly slow secretion. Somatostatin is negative feedback, released by antral acid to stop gastrin release.

notes.h: Digestion of carbohydrate, protein, and fat
points: Salivary and pancreatic amylase cut starch into maltose, maltotriose, and limit dextrins; brush border enzymes (lactase, sucrase, maltase) finish to monosaccharides.
Glucose and galactose enter by SGLT1 with sodium; fructose by GLUT5; all leave the cell by GLUT2.
Enteropeptidase on the duodenal brush border turns trypsinogen into trypsin, which activates the other pancreatic proteases.
Amino acids and di- and tripeptides are absorbed; peptides are split to amino acids inside the cell.
Bile salts emulsify fat; pancreatic lipase with colipase makes fatty acids and monoglycerides, which ride in micelles to the brush border.
Enterocytes rebuild triglycerides and pack them into chylomicrons that enter the lacteals (lymph).
notes.why: Brush border enzymes finish digestion right next to the transporters, so osmotically active small molecules do not pile up in the lumen. SGLT1 is secondary active transport driven by the sodium gradient that the basolateral Na+/K+ ATPase maintains, which is why oral rehydration solution with glucose and sodium works even in cholera. Enteropeptidase sits only on the brush border, which keeps trypsin activation in the duodenum. Fat needs bile salt micelles to cross the unstirred water layer, so ileal resection or pancreatic insufficiency causes steatorrhea and deficiency of vitamins A, D, E, and K.

points: Rectal stretch triggers reflex relaxation of the internal anal sphincter (smooth muscle, myenteric plexus) and the urge to defecate.
The external anal sphincter (skeletal muscle, pudendal nerve S2 to S4) stays closed by choice until the time is right.
Gastrocolic reflex: a filling stomach increases colonic mass movements, which is why the urge often comes after meals.
Pudendal nerve injury weakens the external sphincter and gives urge incontinence; internal sphincter damage gives passive leaking at rest.
notes.why: Rectal distension starts an intrinsic myenteric reflex and a stronger parasympathetic reflex through the sacral cord (pelvic nerves, S2 to S4) that strengthens colonic contraction and relaxes the internal sphincter (the rectoanal inhibitory reflex). The external sphincter is skeletal muscle under voluntary pudendal control, so holding stool depends on squeezing it until the rectum accommodates and the urge fades. The internal sphincter supplies most resting tone, so its damage causes passive leakage, while the external sphincter supplies voluntary squeeze, so its loss causes leakage with urgency when the rectum fills. The rectoanal inhibitory reflex depends on enteric neurons, so it is absent in Hirschsprung disease.

points: The chemoreceptor trigger zone sits in the area postrema, outside the blood-brain barrier, and senses drugs and toxins in blood (D2, 5-HT3, NK1 receptors).
It signals the vomiting center in the medulla, which also gets input from gut vagal afferents, the vestibular system, and the cortex.
Prolonged vomiting loses HCl, causing hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis.
Volume loss turns on aldosterone, which wastes K+ and H+ in the urine, causing hypokalemia and keeping the alkalosis going.
notes.why: The area postrema lies outside the blood-brain barrier, so circulating drugs (such as chemotherapy and opioids), toxins, and uremic products reach its D2, 5-HT3, and NK1 receptors, which is why antiemetics block those receptors. Gut irritation releases serotonin from enterochromaffin cells onto 5-HT3 receptors on vagal afferents, a second route to the vomiting center. Each H+ the parietal cell secretes adds one HCO3- to the blood, so losing gastric HCl in vomitus leaves that bicarbonate behind. Volume loss activates renin, angiotensin, and aldosterone, and the kidney reabsorbs sodium in exchange for K+ and H+ while chloride depletion limits bicarbonate excretion, so the alkalosis persists until saline restores volume and chloride.

Less acid sent to the duodenum

tricks.label: Cell letters and their hormones
tricks.text: G cells make Gastrin, S cells make Secretin, and M cells make Motilin, so those letters match. K cells make GIP and I cells make CCK, so those two need extra practice.

tricks.label: Three keys, one lock
tricks.text: ACh, gastrin, and histamine are three keys that all open the same lock, the H+/K+ ATPase. Block the pump and all three lose their effect.

tricks.label: Lose acid, lose volume, lose potassium
tricks.text: Vomiting removes HCl (alkalosis, low chloride), shrinks volume (aldosterone), and aldosterone makes the kidney dump K+ and H+ (low potassium, worse alkalosis).

highYield: Achalasia: loss of inhibitory (NO and VIP) myenteric neurons, so the lower esophageal sphincter cannot relax and peristalsis is lost.
Erythromycin acts on motilin receptors and speeds gastric emptying.
Enteropeptidase deficiency leaves trypsinogen inactive and causes protein malabsorption.
Oral glucose releases more insulin than the same glucose given by vein because gut incretins (GIP and GLP-1) add to the insulin response.
Fat malabsorption causes steatorrhea and deficiency of vitamins A, D, E, and K.
Bile salts are reabsorbed in the terminal ileum; ileal resection causes bile salt loss and fat malabsorption.
In prolonged vomiting, urine chloride is low and the alkalosis corrects with saline.
pitfalls: Spike potentials riding on slow waves trigger contraction; a slow wave by itself only sets the rhythm.
Secretin brings bicarbonate; CCK brings enzymes and bile.
The internal anal sphincter relaxes by reflex; only the external sphincter is under voluntary control.
Most K+ lost in vomiting leaves through the kidney; gastric fluid itself holds little K+.
The intestinal phase is mostly inhibitory even though a small amount of gastrin comes from the duodenum.

flows.title: Gastric acid secretion and its brake
steps: Vagal GRP, distension, and dietary peptides stimulate antral G cells.
G cells release gastrin into the blood.
Gastrin acts on CCK-B receptors of ECL cells, releasing histamine.
Histamine (H2), gastrin, and ACh (M3) activate parietal cells.
The H+/K+ ATPase pumps H+ into the lumen in exchange for K+.
Low antral pH releases somatostatin from D cells, inhibiting G cells.

flows.title: Fat digestion and absorption
steps: Bile salts emulsify fat into small droplets.
Pancreatic lipase with colipase yields fatty acids and monoglycerides.
Micelles carry these products to the brush border.
Enterocytes resynthesize triglyceride in the smooth endoplasmic reticulum.
Triglyceride is packaged with apoB-48 into chylomicrons.
Chylomicrons leave by exocytosis into lacteals and travel in lymph.

flows.title: Prolonged vomiting to metabolic alkalosis
steps: Vomiting removes gastric HCl, leaving its matching bicarbonate in blood.
Volume loss activates renin, angiotensin, and aldosterone.
Aldosterone increases sodium reabsorption and K+ and H+ secretion.
Hypokalemia and chloride depletion keep bicarbonate reabsorption high.
Result: hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis with paradoxical aciduria.
